questions.problem: Find the value of $c$ that satisfies the mean value theorem for integrals for  $f(x)=2x$ on the interval $[1,3].$
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the mean value theorem for the integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(c)(b-a) & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ f(c) & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3-1}{\int }_{1}^{3}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({x}^{2})|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[{3}^{2}-{1}^{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(9-1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the expression for $f(x)$ to solve for the value of $c:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(c) & =4 \\ 2c & =4 \\ c & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the mean value theorem for the integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(b-a)f(c) & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ f(c) & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ f(c) & =\frac{1}{1-(-1)}{\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{3}-3x+2)\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+2x)|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[(\frac{1}{4}\cdot (1)^{4}-\frac{3}{2}(1)^{2}+2\cdot 1)-(\frac{1}{4}\cdot (-1)^{4}-\frac{3}{2}(-1)^{2}+2\cdot (-1))] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{3}{2}+2)-(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{3}{2}-2)] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{3}{4}-(-\frac{13}{4})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the expression for $f(x)$ to solve for the value of $c:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(c) & =2 \\ {c}^{3}-3c+2 & =2 \\ {c}^{3}-3c & =0 \\ c({c}^{2}-3) & =0 \\ c & =0\,\text{or}\,c=\pm \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

However, since $c\in [-1,1],$ we take only $c=0.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Average Value of a Function Over a Given Interval
questions.problem: Find the average value of the function $f(x)={cos}^{4}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ on the interval $[0,\pi ].$
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi -0}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{4}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate this integral using a substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $-1$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{4}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{\frac{1}{\pi }(\frac{{u}^{5}}{5})|}_{1}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5\pi }[(-1)^{5}-{1}^{5}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{5\pi }(-2) \\  & =\frac{2}{5\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The average value of a function on a given interval $[a,b]$ is 

$$
{f}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the additive property of the definite integral, we write

$$
{\int }_{1}^{9}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{1}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{5}^{9}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{2}}.
$$

The 1st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [1,5].$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have 

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{1}=-4.
$$

The 2nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [5,9].$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 3 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
{\int }_{5}^{9}f(x)\,\text{d}x={A}_{2}=6.
$$

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{9}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} \\  & =-4+6 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the formula for the average value, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9-1}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

\eqalign{
       f(c) (b-a)  & =  \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx \[5pt]
              f(c)    & = \dfrac {1}{b-a} \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx \[5pt]
    & = \dfrac {1}{3-0} \int_0^3  (x^2-2x+2) \, \textrm dx \[5pt]
     & =  \left . \dfrac {1}{3} \cdot  \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3} -x^2 +2x\right] \right|_0^3 \[5pt]
    & =   \dfrac {1}{3} \cdot \left[ \left(\dfrac{3^3}{3} -3^2 +2\cdot3\right) -  \left(\dfrac{0^3}{3} -0^2 +2\cdot0\right)\right] \[5pt]
    & =  \dfrac {1}{3}\cdot6 \[5pt]
    &  = 2.
}
$$

    

Now, we use the expression for $f(x)$ to solve for the value of $c\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(c) & =2 \\ {c}^{2}-2c+2 & =2 \\ c(c-2) & =0 \\ c & =0,2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Average Value of a Function Over a Given Interval
canonical_examples.problem: Find the average value of the function $f(x) = x - 2$ on the interval $[-2, 4].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{b-a}\,{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4-(-2)}{\int }_{-2}^{4}x-2\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-2x){|}_{-2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-2(4))-(\frac{(-2)^{2}}{2}-2(-2))] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[(8-8)-(2+4)] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(0-6) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding an Interval Given the Average Value of a Function
canonical_examples.problem: Find $c$ such that the average value of $g(x) = 3 x$ on the interval $[0,c]$ is equal to $3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To solve for $c,$ we apply the average value formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{b-a}\,{\int }_{a}^{b}g(x)\,\text{d}x \\ 3 & =\frac{1}{c-0}\,{\int }_{0}^{c}3x\,\text{d}x \\ 3 & =\frac{1}{c}(\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}){|}_{0}^{c} \\ 3 & =\frac{1}{c}(\frac{3{c}^{2}}{2}-0) \\ 3 & =\frac{3c}{2} \\ c & =2\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Average Value of a Function Given a Graph
canonical_examples.problem:
The graph of the function $f(x),$ which is defined on $[1,6],$ is shown below. The areas of the regions between the graph and the $x$-axis are $5$ and $2,$ respectively (from left to right). Find the average value of $f(x)$ on $[1,6].$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013500/assets/6433d1ca57ceb334f304e894e2655ef50d987567fbcf219314302bb381fd9a83.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The average value of a function on a given interval is

$$
f_\textrm{avg} = \dfrac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

Here, we see that

$$
\int_{1}^{6} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x = -5 + 2 = -3.
$$

So, applying the average value formula, we find that the average value is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6-1}\cdot (-3) \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
